questions.question:

• So the correct form to be used here is "__**have finished**__**"**.

 ** Usage **

 **Zero**

 A possible condition and its probable result

 A hypothetical condition and its probable result
 Simple past

 **Type 3**
 An unreal past condition and its probable result in the past
 Past perfect
 Perfect conditional
 
 

 **Mixed type**
 An unreal past condition and its probable result in the present
 Past perfect

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/51867102c7c2f369f6e29d2efe025e3b3367c68261ec20262828d84ca5c8f854.png] **__Hinglish__**

questions.question:
**Directions: In the sentence, identify the segment which contains the grammatical error.**

After two months, the phone signals were back at the valley.
questions.solution:
The erroneous part is **at the valley.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The sentence is in **Simple past tense. **
 
• In the last part of the sentence, **'at the valley'** seems **incorrect**. '**At' is used for the specification of place and time. **Valley** **is a large area- not specific.
 
• So we have to replace **'At'** with **'In'.**

Hence, **option 4 is the correct choice. **

** [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] Additional Information__**

 
• **In**, as a preposition of place, is usually used to talk about the position of someone or something inside large places such as countries, continents, big cities etc.

 
 
• She grew up *in* New Zealand.
 
 
 
• **At**, as a preposition of place, is usually used to talk about the position of someone or something inside small and unimportant places such as villages, small towns etc.
 
 
• I'll meet you *at* the pub.
 
 
 
• **At **is also commonly used with proper names such as buildings or organizations.
 
 
• I first met her* at* Harrods.
 
 
• She works *at* the bank.
 
 
 
 
 
• **In**, as a preposition of time, is usually used when talking about parts of the day.
 
 
• I'll see you *in* the morning,* in* the evening,* in* the afternoon.
 
 
 
• **At**, as a preposition of time, is usually used with clock time.
 
 
• My train leaves* at *6.30 am.
 
 
 
• **Note **- As with most so-called "rules" in English there are exceptions- We always say "at" night.
